title: CELPIP General Listening — Practice Test 21
instructions: Listen to the audio for each part and answer the questions. Each audio plays once.

parts.title: Problem Solving
parts.description: A conversation in which one person has a problem and seeks help from another.

parts.title: Daily Life Conversation
parts.description: An everyday conversation between two people.

parts.title: Listening for Information
parts.description: An informational talk; listen for specific details.

parts.title: Discussion
parts.description: A discussion among people with different viewpoints.

parts.title: Viewpoints
parts.description: A longer talk presenting one speaker's opinion and reasons.

listeningScripts.title: A Rescheduled Concert
listeningScripts.text: Caller: The concert I had tickets for was cancelled and moved to March. I can't do March. I'd like a refund. Box office: Let me find the booking. Name and order number? Caller: Adeyemi, order four-four-one-seven-two. Box office: I have it. Two tickets, ninety-four dollars including fees. Caller: The email said tickets remain valid for the new date. Box office: They do, and for a postponement that is usually the end of it. A postponed event doesn't automatically give you a refund. But this one was announced as cancelled first and rescheduled four days later, and in that situation the original cancellation opened a refund window that hasn't closed. Caller: How long is the window? Box office: Thirty days from the cancellation announcement. That was the eleventh, so you have until the tenth of next month. Caller: What about the fees? Box office: The ticket price comes back in full. The booking fee, which is eight dollars of the ninety-four, is the promoter's decision rather than ours, and this promoter does refund it. I would still rather tell you that than let you assume it. Caller: So ninety-four altogether. Box office: Ninety-four altogether, to the card you paid on, in five to seven days. Caller: Do I need to do anything with the tickets themselves? Box office: They're digital, so no. If they had been posted I would need them back before I could process anything, and that catches people out at this time of year. Caller: And if I change my mind about March? Box office: Then don't request the refund. Once it is processed the seats go back on sale immediately, and this show sold out in a morning.

listeningScripts.title: Sharing the School Run
listeningScripts.text: A: Are you still doing both the drop-off and the pick-up? B: Every day. And the pick-up is the one that is killing me. It's twenty past three, which means I stop work at ten to. A: Mine's the same school. Why are we doing this separately? B: Because neither of us asked. What are you thinking? A: I take Mondays and Tuesdays, you take Thursdays and Fridays, and we alternate Wednesdays. B: Alternating anything is how these fall apart. Somebody forgets whose week it is in October, and then it's awkward. A: Then you take Wednesdays, and I'll do a longer Monday. I'll keep them until six that day, so you get an actual afternoon. B: That is more than fair. What about the consent form? A: There is one. The office needs both parents named on each other's collection list, and it has to be signed in person, not scanned. B: When are they open? A: Eight to four. But the office is one person and she is on the gate until nine, so realistically between nine and four. B: I'll go Thursday morning. And if one of us is ill? A: Then we phone the school by two and they hold them in the library. This isn't a favour we're asking each other. It's a system.

listeningScripts.title: Winter Road Maintenance Briefing
listeningScripts.text: Good evening. I am here to explain how the snow route works, because every year we get the same six complaints, and five of them are about things that are working correctly. Priority one is the arterial roads and the hospital routes. Priority two is bus routes and school zones. Priority three is residential streets, and priority three does not begin until priorities one and two are complete, which after a large storm can be thirty-six hours. Your street has not been forgotten. It is third. The plough will leave a ridge across the end of your driveway. I would like to tell you that we can prevent that, and we can't. The snow has to go somewhere, and the blade cannot lift over a driveway. What you can do is clear your snow to the right of the driveway as you face the road, so that the next pass doesn't put it straight back. Do not shovel snow into the street. It is not a bylaw we enjoy enforcing, but a shovelled pile refreezes into an object that a plough hits at forty. Parking. When a snow route is declared, the ban runs from midnight until seven, on the streets marked with the blue signs — not on every street. People assume it is everywhere, and then move a car that never needed moving. And if there is a fire hydrant on your property line, clearing a metre around it is the single most useful thing any resident does all winter. We have three thousand hydrants and eleven staff.

listeningScripts.title: Overnight Heat Warnings
listeningScripts.text: Environment Canada will begin issuing heat warnings based on overnight temperatures as well as daytime highs, a change that takes effect this summer. Until now a warning has depended chiefly on the daytime maximum. Researchers have argued for years that the more dangerous figure is the overnight low, because a body that cannot cool down at night accumulates strain across consecutive days. In the heat event that killed more than six hundred people in British Columbia in twenty twenty-one, the daytime highs were extreme, but the overnight temperatures were the unusual part. Under the new criteria a warning will be issued when the overnight low stays above a regional threshold for two consecutive nights, even if the daytime highs fall below the old trigger. The change is expected to roughly double the number of heat warnings issued in a typical summer. Some meteorologists have raised the risk of warning fatigue, arguing that a warning people stop noticing is worse than no warning at all. The agency responded that its own review found the opposite pattern for heat specifically, though it agreed to monitor it. Municipalities have asked for funding to open cooling centres more often, which is not part of the announcement.

listeningScripts.title: Whether to Charge Museum Admission
listeningScripts.text: Ferreira: We are eighty thousand short for next year. Admission at eight dollars, with under-eighteens free, would raise about a hundred and ten. Rasmussen: On what attendance assumption? Ferreira: Current attendance, less fifteen per cent. Adeyemi: Fifteen is optimistic. Museums that introduced admission in the last decade lost between a quarter and a third, and they did not get it back when they dropped the charge again. Ferreira: Then say twenty-five per cent, and it still raises ninety. Adeyemi: It does. My objection isn't the arithmetic. It's who the twenty-five per cent are. The people who stop coming aren't spread evenly. They are the ones who came in for forty minutes on a wet Saturday because it was free and it was there. That is most of our school-holiday traffic and almost all of our repeat local visitors. Rasmussen: And those are the ones the funder counts. Adeyemi: Exactly. Our grant is renewed on local engagement numbers. We would raise ninety thousand and put a hundred and forty thousand grant at risk. Ferreira: Then that's decisive, and I wish somebody had said it in June. Rasmussen: What about a suggested donation, with a staffed desk? Not a turnstile. Adeyemi: That works elsewhere. It raises about a fifth of what admission would, and it doesn't touch the attendance figure at all. Ferreira: A fifth of a hundred and ten is twenty-two. We need eighty. Rasmussen: Then it is twenty-two from donations, and the rest comes out of the building budget, which means the roof waits another year. Ferreira: I can live with the roof waiting. I can't live with losing the grant.

listeningScripts.title: Body Checking in Youth Hockey
listeningScripts.text: The age at which body checking is introduced in youth hockey has moved twice in fifteen years, and it will probably move again. It is a good case study in how a policy argument changes when somebody finally measures the thing being argued about. The old defence of early checking was a learning argument. Introduce it young, while players are small and slow, and they learn to give and take a hit safely before the collisions become dangerous. It is an intuitive argument. It is also the one the evidence has been least kind to. When one province raised the age from eleven to thirteen and the neighbouring province did not, researchers had something close to a natural experiment. Injury rates in the eleven-to-twelve age group fell by about half. That much was expected. The part that was not expected is what happened when those players turned thirteen and started checking. Their injury rate at thirteen was no higher than the rate among players who had been checking for two years already. The safety-through-early-exposure argument predicted the opposite, and it did not happen. What I would not do is treat that as settling the whole question. The same studies find that concussion rates at every age remain high in absolute terms, and raising the age moves the injuries later rather than removing them. Anybody presenting the age change as having solved something is overreading it. So: raise the age, on the evidence, and keep saying out loud that the sport still has a concussion problem which the age of checking does not fix.

questions.prompt: Why is the caller telephoning?
options: Her tickets did not arrive before the concert
She was charged for more tickets than she ordered
She wants a refund for a concert moved to a date she cannot attend
She wants to change her tickets to a different night
questions.correctAnswer: She wants a refund for a concert moved to a date she cannot attend
questions.explanation: The concert was cancelled and rescheduled to March, which the caller cannot do, so she is asking for her money back rather than the new date.

questions.prompt: What did the email tell her?
options: The tickets stay valid for the rescheduled date
The tickets would be refunded automatically
The tickets had to be exchanged within thirty days
The concert would not be rescheduled
questions.correctAnswer: The tickets stay valid for the rescheduled date
questions.explanation: The email said tickets remain valid for the new date, which is the usual position for a postponement.

questions.prompt: Why is a refund available in this case?
options: The tickets were bought directly from the venue
The new date is more than three months away
The promoter has changed since the booking
The event was announced as cancelled before it was rescheduled
questions.correctAnswer: The event was announced as cancelled before it was rescheduled
questions.explanation: A postponement alone would not give a refund; this event was called off first and rescheduled four days later, and that cancellation opened a refund window.

questions.prompt: How long does the refund window last?
options: Thirty days from the original concert date
Thirty days from the cancellation announcement
Until the rescheduled date in March
Seven days from the request
questions.correctAnswer: Thirty days from the cancellation announcement
questions.explanation: The window is thirty days from the announcement on the eleventh, which leaves the caller until the tenth of next month.

questions.prompt: What is the position on the booking fee?
options: It is never refundable on any booking
The box office refunds it automatically
The promoter decides, and this one does return it
It is refunded only on postponed events
questions.correctAnswer: The promoter decides, and this one does return it
questions.explanation: The ticket price always comes back; the eight-dollar booking fee is the promoter's decision, and this promoter refunds it — which the box office volunteers rather than leaving her to assume.

questions.prompt: How much will the caller receive?
options: Eighty-six dollars
Ninety-four dollars
Forty-seven dollars
Eight dollars
questions.correctAnswer: Ninety-four dollars
questions.explanation: The full ninety-four dollars comes back, including the eight-dollar booking fee, to the card she paid on within five to seven days.

questions.prompt: Why does she not need to do anything with the tickets?
options: They are digital rather than posted
The box office has already cancelled them
The refund is processed before the tickets expire
The venue keeps a record of the order
questions.correctAnswer: They are digital rather than posted
questions.explanation: Digital tickets need nothing; posted ones would have to be returned before the refund could be processed, which the box office says catches people out at this time of year.

questions.prompt: Why should she be certain before requesting the refund?
options: A second refund request cannot be made
The booking fee is not returned twice
The promoter reviews each request individually
The seats go back on sale as soon as it is processed
questions.correctAnswer: The seats go back on sale as soon as it is processed
questions.explanation: Once processed, the seats are released immediately, and the show sold out in a morning — so a change of mind about March would leave her with nothing.

questions.prompt: What is B's difficulty?
options: The school is a long way from B's office
B has no car for the afternoons
The drop-off and pick-up are at different schools
The pick-up time forces B to stop work early
questions.correctAnswer: The pick-up time forces B to stop work early
questions.explanation: The pick-up is at twenty past three, so B stops work at ten to — the part B calls the one that is killing them.

questions.prompt: What does A propose first?
options: Taking the whole week in turn, a week each
Splitting the week, with Wednesdays alternating
Paying a childminder for the afternoons
Asking the school for a later pick-up
questions.correctAnswer: Splitting the week, with Wednesdays alternating
questions.explanation: A's opening suggestion is Mondays and Tuesdays for A, Thursdays and Fridays for B, and alternate Wednesdays.

questions.prompt: Why does B object to that?
options: Wednesdays are B's busiest day
It gives A the easier days
Alternating arrangements collapse once somebody forgets
The school does not allow shared collection
questions.correctAnswer: Alternating arrangements collapse once somebody forgets
questions.explanation: B's view is that alternating anything is how these arrangements fall apart: somebody forgets whose week it is in October and it becomes awkward.

questions.prompt: What do they settle on instead?
options: B takes Wednesdays and A keeps the children later on Mondays
A takes Wednesdays and B takes an extra Friday
They alternate fortnights rather than weeks
They ask a third parent to take Wednesdays
questions.correctAnswer: B takes Wednesdays and A keeps the children later on Mondays
questions.explanation: A gives B all the Wednesdays and balances it with a longer Monday, keeping the children until six so B gets a whole afternoon.

questions.prompt: What has to be done at the school office?
options: A form scanned and emailed before Thursday
A meeting with the head teacher
A collection form signed in person, between nine and four
A letter from each parent's employer
questions.correctAnswer: A collection form signed in person, between nine and four
questions.explanation: Both parents must be named on each other's collection list, signed in person rather than scanned — and although the office opens at eight, the one member of staff is on the gate until nine.

questions.prompt: Which streets are cleared last?
options: Residential streets
Bus routes and school zones
Arterial roads
Streets with fire hydrants
questions.correctAnswer: Residential streets
questions.explanation: Priority one is arterials and hospital routes, priority two is bus routes and school zones, and residential streets are third.

questions.prompt: When does that clearing begin?
options: Thirty-six hours after a storm begins
At the same time as the bus routes
Only once the first two priorities are finished
When residents request it
questions.correctAnswer: Only once the first two priorities are finished
questions.explanation: Priority three does not start until priorities one and two are complete, which after a large storm can be thirty-six hours.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker say cannot be prevented?
options: Ice forming on residential streets
The ridge of snow left across a driveway
Delays of more than thirty-six hours
Cars being towed from snow routes
questions.correctAnswer: The ridge of snow left across a driveway
questions.explanation: The speaker is direct about it: the snow has to go somewhere and the blade cannot lift over a driveway, so the ridge is unavoidable.

questions.prompt: What can residents do to reduce the problem?
options: Clear it to the left of the driveway
Wait until the plough has passed twice
Pile it against the kerb
Clear their snow to the right of the driveway as they face the road
questions.correctAnswer: Clear their snow to the right of the driveway as they face the road
questions.explanation: Clearing to the right as you face the road means the next pass does not push it straight back across the entrance.

questions.prompt: Why must snow not be shovelled into the street?
options: It refreezes into something a plough strikes at speed
It blocks the drains when it melts
It makes the street impassable for buses
It is charged for by weight
questions.correctAnswer: It refreezes into something a plough strikes at speed
questions.explanation: A shovelled pile refreezes into an object that a plough hits at forty — which is why the bylaw exists, even though the speaker dislikes enforcing it.

questions.prompt: What do people misunderstand about the parking ban?
options: It runs all day rather than overnight
It applies only after a storm has ended
It applies only to residential streets
It applies only to streets with blue signs
questions.correctAnswer: It applies only to streets with blue signs
questions.explanation: The ban runs midnight to seven on the streets marked with blue signs, and people assume it covers everywhere and move cars that never needed moving.

questions.prompt: What is changing?
options: Warnings will be issued a day earlier than before
Warnings will take account of overnight temperatures
Daytime thresholds are being lowered
Warnings will be issued by municipalities
questions.correctAnswer: Warnings will take account of overnight temperatures
questions.explanation: Heat warnings will now be based on overnight temperatures as well as daytime highs, from this summer.

questions.prompt: Why do researchers say the overnight figure matters more?
options: Overnight temperatures are easier to forecast
Most heat deaths occur during the night
Daytime highs are already falling
A body that cannot cool at night accumulates strain over several days
questions.correctAnswer: A body that cannot cool at night accumulates strain over several days
questions.explanation: The argument is cumulative: without a cool night the body carries strain into the following day, and it builds across consecutive days.

questions.prompt: What was unusual about the twenty twenty-one heat event?
options: The number of warnings issued
The length of the event
The overnight temperatures
The daytime highs
questions.correctAnswer: The overnight temperatures
questions.explanation: The daytime highs in that event were extreme, but the overnight temperatures were what set it apart.

questions.prompt: What effect is the change expected to have?
options: About twice as many warnings in a typical summer
Fewer but longer warnings
No change to the number of warnings
Warnings restricted to two provinces
questions.correctAnswer: About twice as many warnings in a typical summer
questions.explanation: The new criteria are expected to roughly double the number of heat warnings issued in a typical summer.

questions.prompt: What have municipalities asked for?
options: A delay until next summer
Control over when warnings are issued
A single national threshold rather than regional ones
Money to open cooling centres more often, which the announcement does not cover
questions.correctAnswer: Money to open cooling centres more often, which the announcement does not cover
questions.explanation: Municipalities want funding to open cooling centres more frequently, and that is explicitly not part of the announcement.

questions.prompt: What is the museum's position?
options: It has lost a hundred and ten thousand in grants
Its attendance has fallen by a quarter
It is eighty thousand short for next year
Its roof repair has been cancelled
questions.correctAnswer: It is eighty thousand short for next year
questions.explanation: Ferreira opens with a shortfall of eighty thousand for next year, against which admission at eight dollars would raise about a hundred and ten.

questions.prompt: What attendance does Ferreira's figure assume?
options: Current attendance, less fifteen per cent
Current attendance, unchanged
Current attendance, less a quarter
Attendance from before the pandemic
questions.correctAnswer: Current attendance, less fifteen per cent
questions.explanation: Ferreira's hundred and ten thousand assumes current attendance reduced by fifteen per cent.

questions.prompt: What does Adeyemi say about that assumption?
options: Attendance figures are not measured reliably
Comparable museums lost between a quarter and a third
Free entry has never been shown to raise attendance
The loss would be recovered within two years
questions.correctAnswer: Comparable museums lost between a quarter and a third
questions.explanation: Adeyemi calls fifteen per cent optimistic: museums that introduced admission in the last decade lost a quarter to a third, and did not recover it when the charge was dropped.

questions.prompt: What is Adeyemi's real objection?
options: That eight dollars is too high a price
That under-eighteens should also pay
That the figures were produced too late
Which visitors would be lost, rather than how many
questions.correctAnswer: Which visitors would be lost, rather than how many
questions.explanation: Adeyemi concedes the arithmetic still works at twenty-five per cent, and objects instead to who the lost quarter are: the forty-minute wet-Saturday visitors who make up the school-holiday traffic and the repeat local audience.

questions.prompt: Why does that matter so much?
options: Local visitors spend most in the shop
School groups are booked a year ahead
The museum's grant is renewed on local engagement numbers
The funder inspects on Saturdays
questions.correctAnswer: The museum's grant is renewed on local engagement numbers
questions.explanation: The visitors who would be lost are the ones the funder counts, and the grant — a hundred and forty thousand — is renewed on local engagement numbers.

questions.prompt: What does Rasmussen suggest instead?
options: Admission for visitors from outside the area only
A membership scheme for repeat visitors
Closing one day a week
A suggested donation collected at a staffed desk
questions.correctAnswer: A suggested donation collected at a staffed desk
questions.explanation: Rasmussen proposes a suggested donation with a staffed desk rather than a turnstile, which Adeyemi says works elsewhere.

questions.prompt: How much would that raise?
options: About half of what admission would
About a fifth of what admission would
About the same as admission
Enough to cover the shortfall
questions.correctAnswer: About a fifth of what admission would
questions.explanation: A suggested donation raises about a fifth of admission income — twenty-two thousand against the eighty thousand needed — but leaves attendance untouched.

questions.prompt: What is the consequence of that choice?
options: The roof repair is postponed for another year
The grant is reduced by twenty-two thousand
The museum closes on Saturdays
Admission is introduced the following year
questions.correctAnswer: The roof repair is postponed for another year
questions.explanation: The gap between twenty-two thousand and eighty comes out of the building budget, so the roof waits — which Ferreira accepts in preference to losing the grant.

questions.prompt: What was the old argument for checking early?
options: Early checking makes for a faster game
Coaches prefer to teach it young
Older players are harder to train
Players learn to take a hit safely while they are small and slow
questions.correctAnswer: Players learn to take a hit safely while they are small and slow
questions.explanation: The learning argument held that introducing checking young, before collisions become dangerous, teaches players to give and take a hit safely.

questions.prompt: What made the comparison possible?
options: Two leagues in the same province used different rules
One province raised the age while its neighbour did not
The change was introduced and then reversed
Injury records were kept for fifteen years
questions.correctAnswer: One province raised the age while its neighbour did not
questions.explanation: One province moving the age from eleven to thirteen while the neighbouring province did not gave researchers something close to a natural experiment.

questions.prompt: What happened to injuries among eleven- and twelve-year-olds?
options: They fell by about half
They fell by about a fifth
They stayed roughly the same
They rose slightly
questions.correctAnswer: They fell by about half
questions.explanation: Injury rates in the eleven-to-twelve age group fell by about half, which the speaker says was the expected part of the result.

questions.prompt: What was the unexpected finding?
options: Injuries rose sharply once checking began at thirteen
Injuries fell again at fourteen
Players who started at thirteen were injured no more often than those who had checked for two years
The neighbouring province's rates also fell
questions.correctAnswer: Players who started at thirteen were injured no more often than those who had checked for two years
questions.explanation: The safety-through-early-exposure argument predicted higher injury rates among the delayed group at thirteen, and the rates turned out to be no higher.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker warn against?
options: Trusting a study from a single province
Comparing hockey with other contact sports
Changing the rules again too soon
Treating the change of age as having solved the problem
questions.correctAnswer: Treating the change of age as having solved the problem
questions.explanation: Concussion rates at every age remain high in absolute terms, and raising the age moves injuries later rather than removing them, so presenting the change as a solution is overreading it.

questions.prompt: What is the speaker's position?
options: Raise the age, and treat the question as closed
Leave the age where it is until more evidence arrives
Raise the age, and keep saying the concussion problem remains
Remove checking from youth hockey altogether
questions.correctAnswer: Raise the age, and keep saying the concussion problem remains
questions.explanation: The speaker supports raising the age on the evidence while insisting the sport still has a concussion problem that the age of checking does not fix.
